title: YOU DIDN’T TOUCH THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY SOMETHING HAPPENED IN YOUR HEART?
paragraphs:
YOU DIDN’T TOUCH THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY SOMETHING HAPPENED IN YOUR HEART?
What Happens Spiritually When You Objectify People? The hidden moment when a human being made in God’s image becomes something you consume—and how Jesus can rewrite even this scandal into grace.
There is a kind of sin nobody else has to see.
No hotel room.
No secret meeting.
No physical affair.
No message sent.
No hand ever touches another body.
And yet Jesus walks straight past all of our defenses, enters the place nobody else can inspect, and says:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:28.
That is uncomfortable.
Because Jesus does not merely ask what your hands have done.
He asks what your heart has learned to do with another human being.
And maybe that is where this gets painfully personal.
Maybe you have never thought of yourself as someone who “objectifies people.”
Maybe you simply look.
Scroll.
Imagine.
Replay.
Compare.
Zoom in.
Build fantasies around strangers.
Reduce someone to the parts of them that stimulate you.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps you have even convinced yourself that because nothing physical happened, nothing spiritual happened either.
But what if something has been happening inside you every time you train your eyes to separate a body from the soul who lives inside it?
What if lust is not merely about wanting something forbidden?
What if, at its deepest level, it teaches your heart to look at someone God created as a person and experience them primarily as something for you?
That changes the question.
And it makes Jesus’ words far more serious.
The Greek of Matthew 5:28 is revealing:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν—roughly, “with a view to desiring/lusting after her.”
Jesus is addressing more than the involuntary recognition that another person is physically attractive.
That distinction matters.
Temptation is not identical to sin.
Seeing beauty is not identical to objectification.
An unwanted thought entering your mind is not the same thing as deliberately welcoming it, feeding it, replaying it, and using another person within your imagination.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 makes that unmistakable.
So the Gospel is not asking you to panic because you noticed somebody was attractive.
Jesus is exposing something deeper:
the intentional cultivation of lust.
The gaze that does not merely see a person but begins consuming them internally.
And suddenly this is not simply a conversation about sex.
It is a conversation about what another human being is worth.
Go all the way back to the beginning.
Before pornography.
Before dating apps.
Before advertising discovered that human bodies could sell almost anything.
Before social media turned attention into currency.
Before lust became an industry.
There was this:
וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam betsalmo.
“So God created mankind in His image.”
Genesis 1:27.
That Hebrew word צֶלֶם — tselem means “image.”
This is the foundation we keep forgetting.
The person on your screen is not pixels first.
The woman walking past you is not a body first.
The man whose appearance you are evaluating is not a product first.
The person you are fantasizing about is not a character God placed inside your private imagination.
Human beings bear the image of God.
They have histories you do not know.
Fears you cannot see.
Childhood memories.
Private wounds.
Names spoken by mothers.
Dreams.
Regrets.
Questions.
Tears.
And souls that will stand before God.
Objectification performs a terrible reduction.
It takes someone breathtakingly complex and says:
For this moment, I do not need your story.
I do not need your dignity.
I do not need your fears.
I do not need your consent.
I do not need to know whether your soul is hurting.
I only need what your body can make me feel.
That is why objectification is spiritually dangerous.
Not because physical beauty is evil.
God created bodies.
The Bible does not pretend attraction does not exist.
Scripture can speak openly about marital desire and embodied love.
The problem is not that another person has a body.
The problem begins when your desire makes their personhood disappear.
You stop encountering.
You start consuming.
And consumption changes the consumer.
This is something our generation desperately needs to understand.
Repeated lust does not merely affect how you look at other people.
It can train what you expect from them.
You begin evaluating instead of loving.
Comparing instead of honoring.
Taking instead of giving.
Imagining instead of knowing.
And eventually real human beings can struggle to compete with a fantasy world designed entirely around your preferences.
Real people have boundaries.
Fantasy does not.
Real people have bad days.
Fantasy does not.
Real people age.
Fantasy can always be replaced.
Real people disagree with you.
Fantasy obeys you.
Real intimacy requires patience, sacrifice, communication, faithfulness, forgiveness, and vulnerability.
Objectification asks for almost none of those things.
It simply says:
Give me the feeling.
And that is where lust begins discipling the heart in the opposite direction of Jesus.
Christ teaches us to love people sacrificially.
Lust teaches us to consume them selfishly.
Christ asks, “How can I give?”
Objectification asks, “What can I get?”
Paul describes Christian love with radically different language:
“Love does not seek its own.”
That is the force of οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς in 1 Corinthians 13:5.
Love refuses to make everything about itself.

Then Philippians 2:3–5 drives the blade deeper: believers are called to count others as significant, look not only to their own interests but also to the interests of others, and possess the mind demonstrated supremely in Jesus Christ.
Do you see the collision?
Objectification says:
Your body exists in relation to my appetite.
Christlike love says:
Your dignity matters even when honoring it costs me something.
That is why this cannot simply be solved by “trying harder not to look.”
Something deeper must change.
The heart needs another vision of people.
And another vision of Jesus.
Because there is another danger hiding here.
Shame.
Perhaps you are reading this and realizing how far this has gone.
Maybe pornography has been secretly discipling your imagination for years.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time you looked at certain people without immediately evaluating their bodies.
Maybe you love your spouse, but your imagination constantly compares them with people online.
Maybe you have prayed:
“God, I will never do it again.”
Then you did.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Eventually the prayer changed.
“God, what is wrong with me?”
Then perhaps even that prayer disappeared.
You learned to hide.
Listen carefully now, because this is where many Christian messages become dangerous.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Stay hidden because God is disgusted with you.”
Those are not the same voice.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes repentance possible without pretending your sin is stronger than Christ’s blood.
Jesus does not expose darkness because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what destroys us so He can call us out of it.
Remember the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully cleaned themselves before meeting Him.
He came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He welcomed the morally disgraced.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He forgave the repentant.
And then He walked toward a cross carrying sins He never committed.
Including sexual sin.
Including secret sin.
Including the sins nobody knows about.
Including yours.
At Calvary, Christ was not pretending humanity was cleaner than it was.
The cross is God’s declaration that our condition was so serious the Son of God had to die—and that His mercy was so astonishing He willingly did.
That is scandal.
And then comes grace.
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved.
Power to come home.
Jesus does not merely want you to stop objectifying people.
He wants to restore your ability to see them.
Really see them.
As neighbors.
As brothers and sisters.
As image-bearers.
As people Christ commands you to love.
For the Christian, even your body is no longer simply an instrument for appetite.
Paul asks:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
Then comes the conclusion:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
1 Corinthians 6:19–20.
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Notice what Christianity does.
It does not say bodies are worthless.
It says bodies matter enormously.
Your body matters.
Their body matters.
What you do with your eyes matters.
What you rehearse in your imagination matters.
How you treat people matters.
And because Jesus purchased you at tremendous cost, even your sexuality can become an arena of worship.
Perhaps repentance tonight looks surprisingly ordinary.
Closing the page.
Unfollowing the account.
Deleting what keeps feeding the cycle.
Stopping the second look.
Refusing to mentally undress the stranger.
Talking honestly with a mature Christian you trust instead of fighting indefinitely in secrecy.
Seeking pastoral care or qualified professional help when the pattern has become deeply compulsive.
Praying for the person you were about to consume in your imagination.
Not a dramatic prayer.
Just:
“Jesus, help me see this person the way You do.”
Imagine what might happen if you practiced that.
The person becomes human again.
Not an image.
Not a fantasy.
Not a collection of desirable features.
A person.
Made by God.
Known by God.
Loved enough that Christ calls you to treat them with dignity.
And something begins changing inside you too.
Because every time you refuse to reduce another human being to an object, you are resisting the formation of a selfish heart.
Every time you choose honor over consumption, you are practicing love.
Every time you bring hidden lust into the light and run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him, shame loses another hiding place.
Maybe you will stumble again.
Do not turn that sentence into permission.
Turn it into preparation.
When you fall, repent quickly.
Do not build a house where you fell.
Get up.
Confess.
Return to Christ.
Remove what needs removing.
Seek accountability.
Keep fighting.
First John 1:9 does not say faithful Christians never need confession.
It tells believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
That cleansing is not an excuse to love darkness.
It is a reason to stop hiding there.
Somebody reading this has carried this secret for years.
You love Jesus.
That may be exactly why the contradiction hurts so badly.
You worship on Sunday and fight your browser history during the week.
You know Scripture.
You know the songs.
You know what you should be doing.
And still there is that private battlefield nobody sees.
If that is you, hear this without softening either side of the Gospel:
Your sin is serious.
And Jesus is greater.
Repentance is necessary.
And mercy is available.
You cannot heal what you insist on hiding.
But you also do not have to clean yourself before approaching the One who cleanses sinners.
Bring the scandal to Jesus.
Bring Him the history.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the names.
Bring Him the searches.
Bring Him the habits.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified somebody might discover.
No performance.
No religious editing.
No carefully sanitized confession.
Just truth.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And then walk in repentance.
Maybe that prayer is where your story begins changing.
Sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack in a wall that has been standing for years.
Send it privately to the believer who has been fighting in silence.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God’s favor. Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with your resources, one biblical expression of that desire is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel ministry and helping truth reach other people. Paul teaches the principle that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 9:14, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that Christian giving must never be coerced: “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
Give Jesus your heart.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version everybody else sees.
The real one.
Because the ultimate goal was never merely cleaner browsing history.
It was never merely stronger willpower.
It was never merely becoming respectable enough to say, “At least I am better than those people.”
The goal is Christ.
To become the kind of person who can look into another human face and remember:
You are not here for my consumption.
You bear the image of God.
And I belong to Jesus.
That is what grace does.
It does not merely forgive the eyes that learned to consume.
It begins teaching them how to see again.
And perhaps that is the sentence you should remember when temptation returns:
Jesus did not die merely to change what you look at; He rose again to change the person who is looking.
